To encourage someone means to give them the confidence, support, or motivation they need to do something — to make them feel that they can do it, should do it, or that it is worth doing.

Think of it as a gentle, warm push in a positive direction. You are not forcing anyone. You are not commanding anyone. You are simply making someone feel more capable, more hopeful, or more willing to act.
The Three Main Ways It Is Used

1. To build someone's confidence or spirit

When a person feels afraid, uncertain, or ready to give up, you can encourage them by saying or doing things that make them feel stronger inside.

His coach encouraged him when he wanted to quit.
She encouraged her daughter before the big exam.
The kind words from his friend encouraged him greatly.

Here, encourage means to lift someone's spirit — to make them feel that they are capable and that things will be okay.

2. To actively push someone toward doing something

You can encourage someone to take a specific action by showing enthusiasm, giving reasons, or expressing that you believe it is a good idea. You are not forcing them — you are making the idea feel more appealing or less scary.

The teacher encouraged her students to read more books.
The doctor encouraged him to exercise three times a week.
His parents always encouraged him to follow his passion.

Notice the pattern here: encourage + someone + to + action. This is one of the most common ways the word is used.

3. To make something more likely to happen (used with things, not people)

This is a slightly broader use. Here, the subject doing the "encouraging" is not a person — it could be a condition, a system, a law, or an environment. It simply means to promote or make something easier to happen.

Warm sunlight encourages plant growth.
Praise encourages good behavior in children.
The new policy encourages small businesses to invest.

In these sentences, nobody is consciously choosing to encourage. The sunlight, the praise, and the policy are simply creating conditions that make something more likely.

It is always gentle and positive. You encourage someone toward something, never away. And the tone is always supportive — never forceful, never threatening.

It can be done through words, actions, or simply by creating the right conditions. A parent encourages a child by saying "I believe in you." A government encourages investment by lowering taxes. A smile can encourage a nervous speaker. The method varies widely.

It involves goodwill. When you encourage someone, you genuinely want good things for them. This is what separates it from manipulation or pressure.

• It does not mean to force or compel. Forcing someone removes their choice. Encouraging respects it.
  • It does not mean to command. A command is an order. Encouragement is an invitation.
  • It does not mean to pressure or stress someone. Pressure implies tension. Encouragement implies warmth.
  • It does not mean to flatter falsely. Genuine encouragement is honest and caring.
Degrees of Meaning: Where Does "Encourage" Sit?

Think of a scale of intensity:

suggest → encourage → urge → pressure → force

"Encourage" sits comfortably in the gentle middle. It is stronger than a passing suggestion, but far softer than urging or pressuring. It carries a sense of care and belief in the other person.
How to Use It: Common Sentence Patterns

PatternExample

encourage + someone + to + verb

She encouraged me to apply for the job.

encourage + someone + in + something

He always encouraged her in her art.

(This means he supported her ongoing effort in art.)

encourage + noun (a thing)

The new rules encourage transparency.

be encouraged

I was encouraged by his kind words.

(Means: his words gave me confidence or hope.)

feel encouraged

She felt encouraged after the meeting.

(Means: she left feeling more hopeful and motivated.)

Motivate — focuses on giving someone energy or drive from within. You motivate someone by connecting to what they already care about. Encourage is softer and more about emotional support.

Inspire — more powerful and emotional. Inspiration often involves awe or deep feeling. Encouragement is more everyday and personal.

Support — broader. Support can mean practical help (money, presence, resources). Encourage focuses specifically on the emotional or motivational boost.

Urge — stronger than encourage. When you urge someone, you are insisting more firmly. Encourage is gentler.

Foster — means to nurture something slowly over time, often used for qualities, environments, or relationships. Foster creativity means to build it gradually. Encourage creativity means to support or promote it.
A Few More Examples Across Different Contexts

In education:

Good teachers don't just teach facts — they encourage students to think for themselves.

In health:

The nutritionist encouraged her to eat more vegetables and drink enough water.

In work:

The manager encouraged her team to share ideas freely without fear of judgment.

In society:

Scholarships encourage talented students from poor families to pursue higher education.

In personal relationships:

Even when he failed, his best friend always encouraged him to try again.

In nature/science (figurative):

Moisture in the soil encourages the roots to grow deeper.

When someone encourages you, you feel seen, believed in, and supported. You feel less alone in your effort. You feel that someone is in your corner — not doing the work for you, but rooting for you.

When you encourage someone else, you are giving them a gift that costs you nothing but means a great deal to them. It is one of the most human and generous acts in language.

In one sentence: To encourage means to give someone (or something) the support, confidence, or favorable conditions needed to do something — through words, actions, or by simply creating the right environment — always gently, always positively, never by force.
